questions.q: What type does TypeScript infer for currency?
questions.explain: A const binding can never be reassigned, so the most precise type, the literal type "NGN", is safe. That is literal inference.
questions.code: const currency = "NGN";

questions.q: What type does TypeScript infer for currency here?
questions.explain: A let can be reassigned later, so the literal type is widened to string. Otherwise currency = "USD" would be an error.
questions.code: let currency = "NGN";

questions.q: What is the type of order.status?
questions.explain: The const only stops order itself from being reassigned. Its properties can still change (order.status = "refunded"), so they widen: status is string.
questions.code: const order = { id: 1042, status: "paid" };

questions.q: What is the type of fee?
questions.explain: An annotation is the declared type and it wins. TypeScript checks that 50 fits number, then treats fee as a number from then on.
questions.code: const fee: number = 50;
options: It depends on how fee is used later

questions.q: What type does as const give roles?
questions.explain: A const assertion stops widening at every level and makes arrays and properties readonly. The array becomes a readonly tuple of the exact strings, in order.
questions.code: const roles = ["customer", "teller", "manager"] as const;

questions.q: What type does TypeScript infer for lines?
questions.explain: For an array, TypeScript builds the best common type of all elements, which here is a union, and widens the literals because arrays can change. It never infers a tuple on its own; you write the tuple type or use as const.
questions.code: const lines = [2500, "delivery", 700];

questions.q: What type does TypeScript infer for fee?
questions.explain: A conditional expression has the union of its two branch types. Because fee is a const, the literals are kept. TypeScript 7 may print the members in a different order, which means nothing.
questions.code:
declare const isVip: boolean;
const fee = isVip ? 0 : "standard";

questions.q: Why should you write const pending: Transfer[] = [] instead of const pending = []?
questions.explain: An unannotated empty array's type grows with each push. The type of a list should be decided by you, not by the first value someone happens to add.
options: Because empty arrays are not allowed without a type
Because an empty array gives inference nothing to go on: its type would evolve with whatever is pushed first
Because const arrays cannot be pushed to without an annotation
Because it makes the array faster

questions.q: What does strict report here?
questions.explain: A let starting as null gets an evolving type. Inside another function TypeScript cannot know which assignment happened, so there it is any, which strict mode reports. Annotate it: let approvedBy: string | null = null.
options: TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'string'
That approvedBy implicitly has type any (TS7034 and TS7005)

questions.q: Why does orders.filter((o) => o.total > 10000) need no annotation on o?
questions.explain: That is contextual typing: the type flows from the place the expression is written into the expression. filter's declaration says it calls the callback with an element, so o is an Order.
options: Because arrow functions never need parameter types
Because the callback is written where filter expects a function taking an element of the array, so o gets that type from the context

questions.q: Why does this report TS7006 "Parameter 'o' implicitly has an 'any' type"?
questions.explain: Context only reaches an expression written in the place that has the expected type. Fix it with (o: Order) => … or by typing the variable: const isLarge: (o: Order) => boolean = ….
questions.code:
const isLarge = (o) => o.total > 10000;
console.log(orders.filter(isLarge));
options: Because filter cannot take a named function
Because the arrow function is declared on its own line, where there is no expected type; the later call to filter does not give it context
Because const functions need a return type

questions.q: ship({ id: 1, status: "paid" }) compiles, but const o = { id: 1, status: "paid" }; ship(o); does not, where ship expects status: "pending" | "paid". Why?
questions.explain: Same value, different type. Where an expected type exists, literals are checked against it and not widened. On its own line, o.status becomes string, which is wider than the union.
options: Because inline objects are not type checked
Because the inline object is contextually typed by the parameter, so "paid" stays a literal; the separate const o is inferred on its own and its property widens to string

questions.q: What return type does TypeScript infer for discount?
questions.explain: Return literals widen to number, and the path that falls off the end returns undefined. Without a return type annotation this compiles, and the error shows up at a caller that tries to multiply by the result.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of writing : number as the return type of discount above?
questions.explain: A return type is a promise the compiler holds the function to. It also stops the function's public type from changing silently when someone edits the body.
options: The compiler reports the missing return inside discount (TS2366), where the bug is, instead of at distant callers

questions.q: An exported function has no return type annotation. A teammate adds return "free" in one branch. What can happen?
questions.explain: An inferred return type is whatever the body returns today. For exported functions it is part of the public API, so write it down and it only changes when you mean it to.
options: Nothing, because return types are checked at runtime
The inferred return type silently becomes a union including "free", and callers across the project may break or behave differently
TypeScript refuses the new return because it differs from the others
The new branch is ignored by inference

questions.q: Which of these is the best place to add an annotation?
questions.explain: Annotate at boundaries, infer inside. Parameters have nothing to infer from and form the contract with callers. The other three are inferred exactly already.
options: The parameters of an exported priceOrder(items, coupon) function

questions.q: What is wrong with const fees: Record<string, number> = { transfer: 10, withdrawal: 25 }; when the keys are fixed?
questions.explain: An annotation wider than the value throws information away. Leave it to inference, or use satisfies Record<string, number> to check the values while keeping the exact keys.
options: Nothing, it is the most precise type
The annotation says any string is a key, so a typo such as fees.tranfer compiles and gives undefined at runtime

questions.q: What does satisfies do in const fees = { transfer: 10 } satisfies Record<string, number>?
questions.explain: satisfies gives you the check of an annotation without its widening. fees.tranfer is then an error, and so is a fee written as a string.
options: It converts the object into a Record at runtime
It replaces the inferred type with Record<string, number>
It checks the value against the type but keeps the inferred type, so fees still has exactly the key transfer

questions.q: When is Record<K, V> as an annotation a good choice?
questions.explain: With a union of keys, Record is precise: forgetting a key is an error and typos are errors. With string keys it only fits data whose keys really are unknown until runtime.
options: When K is a fixed union such as "sms" | "email" | "push": every key is then required and every value gets contextual typing

questions.q: Why should you write string and not String as a parameter type?
questions.explain: The lowercase name is the primitive type. The capitalised one describes the wrapper object (and anything with the string methods), so wrapper objects can slip in. TypeScript even says: "Prefer using 'string' when possible."
options: They are identical; it is only style
String also accepts wrapper objects created with new String(…), which compare by identity and behave differently; string accepts only real strings
String is not allowed in strict mode

questions.q: What is the purpose of writing const probe: never = value; while learning?
questions.explain: The error text is the compiler's own description of the value's type. An editor's hover shows the same thing; delete the probe once you have seen it.
options: Nothing can be assigned to never, so the compiler's error message shows the type it inferred for value

questions.q: What return type is inferred here?
questions.explain: The conditional's type is the union of both literals, and a function's return type is not widened the way a let is. Callers get a precise union they can check exhaustively.

questions.q: A function returns { ok: true, left: 500 } in one branch and { ok: false, reason: "insufficient funds" } in another, with no annotation. What is the practical problem with the inferred type?
questions.explain: TypeScript normalises the shapes (adding left?: undefined and reason?: undefined) and widens true/false. Name a discriminated union yourself, with ok: true and ok: false, as the next lessons show.
options: ok is widened to boolean in both shapes, so checking result.ok does not tell TypeScript which shape you have
Both objects lose all their properties

questions.q: as const made the compiler treat limits as readonly. What does this print at runtime?
questions.explain: as const is erased. It only changes what the compiler allows; the object is an ordinary, unfrozen object at runtime. Use Object.freeze when the runtime must enforce it.
questions.code:
const limits = { daily: 500000, single: 100000 } as const;

console.log(Object.isFrozen(limits), limits.daily);

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: fees.withdrawl is a typo, but the Record<string, number> annotation says every key exists. At runtime it is undefined, and 5010 + undefined is NaN.

questions.q: This compiles, because the return type is inferred. What does it print?
questions.explain: For Kano the function falls off the end and returns undefined. The inferred type is number | undefined, and a template string accepts both, so nothing complains.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Wrapper objects are objects: === compares identity, and two separate objects are never identical. == converts the wrapper to its primitive first, so a == "NGN" is true. typeof says "object".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every object is truthy, including a Boolean wrapper holding false. valueOf() gives back the primitive false. Another reason to write boolean, never Boolean.

questions.q: Widening is a compile-time idea. What does this print?
questions.explain: status is inferred as string, so assigning "paid" is allowed. At runtime both variables are ordinary strings, so their typeof is the same. Literal types and widening only exist for the compiler.
options: It does not compile: status is "pending"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each handler gets id: number from the Record annotation, and the map callback gets s and i from the array. The ids passed are i + 1: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 9500 × 1 + 2800 × 2 = 15100. 7.5% of that is 1132.5, which rounds to 1133. sum is a number because the starting value 0 gives it context, so + adds instead of joining strings.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The annotation gives the empty array its element type, so both pushes are checked. join("+") puts a plus sign between the amounts as text; it does not add them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: as const keeps the exact strings, and (typeof roles)[number] turns them into the union Role. At runtime roles is a normal array: "teller" is at index 1.

questions.q: This does not compile, because order.status widens to string. Fix it with an annotation so it prints order #1042 shipped.
questions.explain: Annotating order as Order checks the object where it is written and gives status the union type, so it can move on to "shipped" later. as const would also compile, but would make the status readonly.

questions.q: Give discount a return type of number and fix what the compiler then reports: orders under ₦5,000 get no discount. Print the amounts to pay for 60000, 8000 and 3000.
questions.explain: With the annotation, TS2366 points inside the function at the missing path. The starter prints NaN for 3000, because 3000 * undefined is NaN.

questions.q: Replace the Record<string, number> annotation with satisfies so typos in keys become compile errors, fix the typo, and print the total fees for one transfer and one withdrawal: 35.
questions.explain: satisfies checks that every value is a number, but keeps the inferred type with exactly two keys, so fees.withdrawl is reported as TS2551. The starter prints NaN.
questions.starter:
const fees: Record<string, number> = { transfer: 10, withdrawal: 25 };

console.log(fees.transfer + fees.withdrawl);
questions.solution:
const fees = { transfer: 10, withdrawal: 25 } satisfies Record<string, number>;

console.log(fees.transfer + fees.withdrawal);

questions.q: Type notifiers once with Record so the three functions need no parameter annotations and every channel is required. Print the two lines shown.
questions.explain: The Record<Channel, …> annotation gives each arrow function its parameter types by contextual typing, and a missing push entry would be an error.
questions.expected:
SMS to Ada: PIN changed
Push to Bola: Transfer received

questions.q: Give the empty entries array a type, then add a credit of 5000 and a debit of 1200, and print the balance 3800.
questions.explain: An empty array gives inference nothing to work with, so annotate it. The objects pushed later are then checked against Entry, including the kind literal.

questions.q: Annotate approvedBy so it may hold a name or null, and write describe() that prints not approved yet or approved by Ada.
questions.explain: Without the annotation, approvedBy has an evolving type that is any inside describe. With string | null, the declaration documents both states, and the === null check handles the empty one.
questions.expected:
not approved yet
approved by Ada

questions.q: Make currencies keep its exact strings with as const, derive a Currency type from it, and write format(amount: number, currency: Currency). Print NGN 2500 | USD 12.
questions.explain: Without as const the array is string[] and (typeof currencies)[number] would just be string. With it, Currency is "NGN" | "USD", and format(5, "EUR") would not compile.

questions.q: The callback lost its context when it was moved into a variable. Give the variable a function type (not a parameter annotation) and print the ids of orders over ₦10,000: [ 1, 3 ].
questions.explain: Typing the variable gives the arrow function its context back, so o is an Order without annotating the parameter itself. (The starter also had the limit wrong by a zero, and printed an empty array.)
